newsitem.title: INDIA: Profit-taking caps early rally in Bombay stocks.
newsitem.headline: Profit-taking caps early rally in Bombay stocks.

text.p: Bombay blue chips on Friday ended off a sharp morning rally as profit-taking on the last day of weekly account pared gains, traders said.
The Bombay share index ended 16.40 points, or 0.44 percent, higher at 3,769.90 provisional, off 3,812.82 intra-day high.
Focus remained on bank stocks that have caught market fancy buoyed by hopes of economic revival, they said.
"We saw profit-taking in these (bank) stocks," said Kuntal Shah, chief dealer at broker D.T. Gandhi. "The market ended flat, but the outlook remains positive."
The rally in Bombay shares came after strong demand for blue chips pushed up stocks at the National Stock Exchange on Thursday. The BSE was closed Thursday for a local holiday.

India's lower house of parliament on Friday approved the 1997/98 (April-March) Finance Bill, the cornerstone of the centre-left government's market-friendly budget proposals that slashed taxes and tariffs.
The final passage of the budget spelt good news for the market and would infuse confidence among foreign investors, traders said.
The budget has been hostage to political developments since its presentation on February 28.
"The market can look forward to focus on positive factors such as monsoon forecasts, as the budget uncertainty is finally over," said an equities dealer at a foreign brokerage.
Shares of Century Textiles and Industries plunged 10 percent on Friday, taking the fall to 24 percent since Monday, after the firm said its profits dropped 99 percent, brokers said.
The share was down 203.25 rupees, or 10 percent, at 1,830 on the Bombay Stock Exchange. On Monday, it closed at 2,401.
The diversified firm said on Tuesday its net profits tumbled to 26.7 million rupees in the year ended March 31, 1997, from 1.9 billion a year ago.
A 218.6 percent jump in interest and finance costs, sluggish cement and paper markets, weak dry bulk freight rates in shipping and acute electricity shortages hit Century operations.
